checks.title: A bare worktree is enough to build and test one change
checks.why: Out of the box, each change gets a fresh copy of the repo and nothing else. If a build here also needs a database, a container, a free port or a credential, that is not enough, and this repo has to supply the extra setup itself.
checks.ask: Starting from a fresh git worktree of this repo and nothing else, can someone build it and run its tests?

checks.title: Three builds can run at once without colliding
checks.why: Up to three changes are worked at the same time. If two builds share a port, a database name, a lock file or a fixed output directory, they corrupt each other and the failures look random.
checks.ask: Can three builds of this repo run at the same time without sharing a port, a database name or an output directory?

checks.title: Commands build the whole product
checks.why: The agent has to build before it can report pass or fail. It does not have to be ONE command: an ordered list is fine, and a repo with a front end and a back end normally needs one for each. What matters is that the list covers every part, and that each step is a command someone can run rather than a written recipe that drifts away from what CI actually runs.
checks.ask: What commands build this product, and in what order? A short list is fine, so say if the front end and the back end build separately. Between them, do they cover every part?

checks.title: Commands run the tests for the whole product
checks.why: A check that cannot run the tests reports a pass that means nothing. This is the one the whole engine leans on: the loops stop at a green PR and never work out for themselves whether the change was correct. One command or a short ordered list, so long as no part of the product is left untested.
checks.ask: What commands run this repo's tests, and in what order? A short list is fine, so say if the front end and the back end have separate suites. Between them, do they cover every part?

checks.title: Commands lint the whole product, and fail on error
checks.why: Lint is the cheapest signal an agent has that it wrote something unidiomatic. A linter that only warns is one an agent learns to ignore. One command or a short ordered list, so long as every part is covered and each step exits non-zero on an error.
checks.ask: What commands lint this repo, and in what order? A short list is fine. Does each one exit non-zero on an error, and do they cover every part?

checks.title: The build is free of warnings today
checks.why: An agent cannot tell the one warning it just introduced from the four hundred that were already there. A noisy baseline turns a real signal into wallpaper.
checks.ask: Run every one of those build commands today. Do they all finish with zero warnings?

checks.title: Something reviews a change before it is pushed
checks.why: Code review and security review happen while a change is being checked, and the loops require only that they happened. A check that builds and tests but reviews nothing quietly drops a gate everyone believes held, so it has to say which reviews actually ran.
checks.ask: What reviews a change in this repo before it reaches a PR: a reviewer agent, a security scan, a required human?

checks.title: Integration tests cover the seams unit tests cannot
checks.why: Unit tests pass on changes that break the moment two components meet. Where this repo has real seams (a database, an HTTP boundary, a plugin host), unit tests alone let an agent ship a plausible break.
checks.ask: Are there integration tests covering the seams between components here?

checks.title: End-to-end tests exist, or a skill explains how to navigate the product
checks.why: An agent that cannot drive the product cannot tell whether its change works in the thing a person uses. End-to-end tests are the strong form; a skill describing how to reach each screen is the weak one, and it is far better than nothing.
checks.ask: Can an agent drive this product end to end: real tests, or a skill telling it how to navigate?

checks.title: Browser tests go through page objects, not raw selectors
checks.why: A test full of raw selectors breaks on every markup change, and an agent asked to fix it edits the selector rather than the bug. Page objects give it one place to look.
checks.ask: Do the browser tests here go through page objects, or do they reach for raw selectors?

checks.title: Coding standards are written down and reachable from CLAUDE.md
checks.why: Standards that live in reviewers' heads cannot reach an agent. Written down but unreferenced is nearly as bad: nothing loads them.
checks.ask: Are this repo's coding standards written down, and does CLAUDE.md point at them?

checks.title: A change that alters the UI has a defined approval path
checks.why: Nothing in the automated chain can judge whether a screen looks right. Without a named path, a UI change either stalls or lands unreviewed, and neither shows up as a failure.
checks.ask: When a change alters the UI, who approves the look of it, and how does the loop reach them?

checks.title: An agent can read whether a build passed
checks.why: Landing a change waits for CI to go green, so an agent that cannot read the build result never lands anything and never says why. The repo fact is WHERE CI runs. On GitHub checks the same access that reads the pull request reads the build, and this costs nothing. Anywhere else it is a second system with its own access, and that is work this repo has to account for before the loops are any use.
checks.ask: Where does CI run, and can an agent read a build result there without a person fetching it?

checks.title: The harness validates its own work before reporting pass
checks.why: A check that reports pass without having run the lint and the tests is the failure this engine is built to prevent: it looks exactly like the working path.

any_file_contains.pattern: dotnet test|dotnet format|npm test|npm run test|npm run lint|yarn test|yarn lint|pnpm test|pnpm lint|pytest|eslint|stylelint
dotnet test|dotnet format|npm test|npm run test|npm run lint|yarn test|yarn lint|pnpm test|pnpm lint|pytest|eslint|stylelint
dotnet test|dotnet format|npm test|npm run test|npm run lint|yarn test|yarn lint|pnpm test|pnpm lint|pytest|eslint|stylelint

checks.ask: Before a change is pushed, should the agent run the lint and the full test command itself rather than leaving it to CI?

checks.title: The branch model is written down
checks.why: Setting this repo up asks a person to confirm which version lines are live and which one is the main one. If nobody has written the branch model down, nobody can confirm it, and a wrong answer sends every change to the wrong branch with nothing failing.
checks.ask: Is this repo's branching strategy written down somewhere an agent can read?

checks.title: The version lives in a known file
checks.why: Cutting a release has to raise the version number. If the version is spread across several files, or only exists as a tag someone types by hand, that step cannot be written down and a release goes out mislabelled.
checks.ask: Which file holds the version this repo publishes under?

checks.title: Something already knows how to prepare a release
checks.why: Preparing a release (branch, bump, changelog, open the PR) is the half nothing generic can guess. A script or skill that already does it here is what the release step should hand off to.
checks.ask: What prepares a release here today: a script, a skill, or a person following notes?

checks.title: Something already knows how to publish a release
checks.why: Publishing must leave nothing half-published when it fails. Where a pipeline already publishes, the honest thing to do is wait for it and report what happened; where nothing does, publishing has to be written from scratch, and that is the riskiest step of the lot.
checks.ask: What publishes a release here: which pipeline, feed or command?

checks.title: After a release, the branches get put back in step
checks.why: This is the step manual releases most often forget, which is exactly why the engine has an action for it. If nobody does it today, the next change starts from something other than what shipped.
checks.ask: After a release here, what merges it back and publishes the notes?

checks.title: Commit messages follow a convention a machine can read
checks.why: Working out the next version usually means reading the commits since the last one, so a fix and a breaking change have to be tellable apart without a person reading each one. Where nothing enforces the format, most commits follow it and the few that do not are the ones that decide the version wrongly.
checks.ask: Do commit messages here follow a set convention, and does anything enforce it?

checks.title: Failures get recorded so the process improves
checks.why: A lesson from a bad run gets filed as an issue and swept up weekly. A repo with nowhere to put a lesson loses every one of them, and repeats the failure at the same cost.
checks.ask: When an automated run goes wrong here, where does the lesson get written down?

checks.title: An issue carries enough for an agent to act on
checks.why: Every loop starts by reading an issue, and that issue is the whole brief. Two lines with no acceptance criteria means the agent guesses and a person reviews the guess, which costs more than writing the issue properly would have.
checks.ask: Where do the issues the loops will read live, and do they carry enough to act on without asking?

checks.title: Line endings are settled, so a diff shows only what changed
checks.why: An agent running on Linux against a repo with no rule rewrites the line endings of every file it touches. The diff then shows the whole file as changed, review becomes impossible, and the loop looks like it rewrote something it only edited one line of.
checks.ask: Does this repo pin its line endings, so a change made on another operating system does not rewrite whole files?

checks.title: The tools the team relies on are reachable by an agent
checks.why: Anything a human needs to do this work and an agent cannot reach becomes a silent ceiling on what the loops can finish.
checks.ask: Which tools does your team use for this repo that an agent currently has no way to reach?

checks.title: Repeated patterns get promoted into written standards
checks.why: A pattern used forty times and written down nowhere is a convention an agent will break, plausibly, in every new file.
checks.ask: Is there anything that turns repeated patterns in this codebase into documented standards?
